paper_title: Lost in the Hallway: Benchmarking Persistent Spatial Memory Across Revisits

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Persistent spatial understanding is essential for embodied agents to operate reliably in environments they repeatedly encounter. It requires recognizing revisited places despite viewpoint changes, distinguishing them from similar-looking rooms, and updating memories as environments change. Yet existing evaluations often leave physical place identity across separated visits implicit. We introduce ReSpaceBench, a benchmark comprising 3,244 questions across 590 synthetic and real-home scenes, organized into 9 tasks spanning room association, persistent state tracking, and downstream reasoning. Controlled walkthroughs define visits by physical room entry and deliberately include same-type room distractors and cross-session object changes. Our evaluation of 32 models and 3 agentic video-understanding frameworks reveals substantial limitations: the strongest evaluated zero-shot model achieves 50.5% overall accuracy and 52.2% on a 450-question subset, compared with 90.1% for human annotators. The evaluated agentic frameworks offer no overall improvement over direct inference with the same base model. Analysis of agent execution traces reveals evidence omissions and incorrect cross-visit room associations as major failure modes, suggesting that iterative evidence seeking alone does not ensure consistent spatial memory. Further analyses expose a gap between recognizing familiar rooms and identifying the correct visited room, while annotation-guided sampling highlights the importance of preserving intervening visits and transitions. We also provide RS-30K, a separate training dataset from synthetic sources with no template, scene, route, or video overlap with the benchmark. Fine-tuning Qwen3-VL-8B raises overall accuracy from 35.5% to 60.4%, with the largest gains in association and improvements extending to real-life scenes.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Embodied agents repeatedly encounter the same physical environments during everyday activities [24, 28]. robot or wearable assistant may return to room from different viewpoint, after visiting other spaces, or after its contents have changed. To build on past experience during these revisits, it must associate new observations with the correct physical place and update its spatial memory accordingly [27, 30, 49]. Yet viewpoint variation can make even familiar room appear substantially different across visits, complicating 1 Figure 1 Challenges in spatial memory across revisits. Left: Three challenges arise when revisiting previously explored environment: (1) Viewpoint Variation: recognizing the same room from different viewpoints; (2) Identity Ambiguity: distinguishing between visually similar but distinct rooms; and (3) State Changes: tracking changes within the same room across repeated visits. Right: Human and MLLM accuracy across all 9 tasks of ReSpaceBench-mini (450 questions). Even the best-performing model remains substantially below human performance. place recognition [20, 37, 68]. Conversely, different rooms may look alike, creating identity ambiguity about the correct identity of the room being revisited [37, 72]. Over time, the agent must also track state changes in the rooms contents and update the corresponding memory [29, 40]. Revisits therefore test whether systems can preserve place identity while tracking changes across temporal observations  (Fig. 1)  . Recent benchmarks have expanded the evaluation of multimodal large language models (MLLMs) from single-image 3D relations to video-based spatial reasoning and long-horizon memory [31, 35, 39, 60]. Yet models still struggle with global cognitive maps, cross-view correspondence, and coherent spatial memory [34, 35, 60, 66]. Cross-visit place association, task well studied in robotics through loop closure and visual place recognition [8, 37], remains largely implicit in the spatial understanding task evaluations. Recent benchmarks, UCS-Bench [53] and SpaMEM [34] evaluate persistent spatial reasoning and memory under scene changes, while LongSpace-Bench [31] covers scene consistency and long-horizon recall; however, none establishes dedicated protocol for room re-identification across controlled revisits. OVO-S-Bench [33] includes revisit detection and counting, but defines visits by whether location enters the field of view, allowing room briefly glimpsed during camera turn to count without physical entry. Its construction also does not systematically control same-type rooms as competing identities. Thus, associating observations with specific physical rooms across controlled revisits remains under-explored. We present ReSpaceBench, benchmark for persistent spatial understanding across revisits. Its 9 tasks span three task families: association, recognizing previously visited rooms and matching them to earlier observations; persistent state, maintaining and updating room and object memories; and downstream reasoning, recovering temporal order and spatial topology. Walkthroughs follow controlled routes, with visits defined by physical room entry rather than visual observation. We select homes with spaces of the same type to serve as identity distractors, testing whether models recognize specific place rather than merely remembering its semantic category. We construct ReSpaceBench from synthetic homes in 3D-FRONT [19] and ProcTHOR [13], real homes scanned with FARO laser scanners [17], and egocentric videos recorded with PICO headset [42]. Using annotated scene metadata and constructed navigation meshes, we use our designed question templates to generate task-conditioned routes: each template specifies both the question and the navigation requirements needed to answer it. The resulting route trajectories include egocentric videos with repeated room visits. We generate answers from metadata, then apply rule-based checks with human verification to remove question answer pairs that are inconsistent with the video. sections.title: Video
sections.content: ReSpaceBench comprises 590 scenes, 3,037 rooms, 353.4 hrs, and 3,244 questions. Our evaluation of 32 models and three agentic video-understanding frameworks (Section 4) reveals substantial limitations in persistent spatial memory. Proprietary models remains the strongest zeroshot models in our evaluation, while specialized spatial and video models do not consistently outperform open-source generalpurpose MLLMs. The evaluated agentic frameworks offer no overall gains over direct inference. On shared 450-question subset, humans achieve 90.1% accuracy compared with 52.2% for the strongest evaluated zero-shot model GPT-5.6 Sol. Further analysis of the six proprietary models on query-to-memory association shows that wrong-room selections account for 66.588.3% of their errors, exposing gap between recognizing room as familiar and identifying the correct visited room. To support model development, we also provide 30k training questions from ProcTHOR training scenes with no scene, route, or video overlap with the benchmark. Fine-tuning Qwen3-VL-8B on this dataset raises overall accuracy from 35.5% to 60.4%, with the largest gains in association and smaller, less consistent gains in state tracking and reasoning. Our contributions are as follows. benchmark for persistent spatial memory. We introduce ReSpaceBench, comprising 9 tasks in 3 task families across synthetic and real homes. Controlled revisits, same-type room distractors, and cross-session state changes support explicit evaluation of room association, persistent state tracking, and downstream spatial reasoning. systematic evaluation and error analysis. We evaluate 32 models and 3 agentic video-understanding frameworks, with human performance reference on shared subset. Detailed analyses of room-association errors, agentic failures, and evidence coverage identify recurring limitations in maintaining and using spatial memory across revisits. training dataset. We release 30k training samples generated from ProcTHOR scenes, with no template, scene, route or video overlap with the benchmark. targeted fine-tuning study demonstrates their utility for developing models with stronger persistent spatial memory.

sections.title: 2.1 Long-context visual retrieval.
sections.content: Long-context evaluations examine whether models can retrieve and combine sparse visual evidence from extended multimodal inputs. Visual Haystacks tests visual needle retrieval and cross-image reasoning, revealing sensitivity to evidence position [57]. MMLongBench broadens evaluation to diverse interleaved visionlanguage tasks at controlled context lengths [54], while Video-LevelGauge systematically probes positional bias in video contexts [58]. Recently, agentic video-understanding frameworks such as AVP, DVD, and VideoAgent use tools to retrieve and inspect video evidence [52, 56, 71]. Retrieving relevant observations, however, does not establish whether they refer to the same physical room across separate visits. ReSpaceBench explicitly evaluates this cross-visit room association over long visual contexts.

sections.title: 2.2 Spatial intelligence and long-horizon memory.
sections.content: Recent benchmarks address complementary aspects of spatial intelligence and long-horizon memory. SpaMEM studies spatial belief updates and object-identity continuity under action-conditioned scene changes in ProcTHOR [34], while UCS-Bench evaluates continual spatial reasoning relative to users changing locations in egocentric streams [53]. EgoMemReason probes entity, event, and behavioral memory over week-long videos [55], and 3DMem-Bench evaluates memory-dependent question answering and embodied tasks in dynamic 3D environments [25]. MMSI-Video-Bench includes cross-video spatial reasoning [35]. All-Angles Bench [66] and SpaCE-10 [22] evaluate multi-view and compositional spatial understanding of static scene from several images, and SAW-Bench [32] evaluates situated awareness in egocentric videos, including changes between two videos of the same scene. However, these benchmarks do not systematically evaluate whether models can recognize physical room when it is revisited. In generative world modeling, MemoBench evaluates whether video generators recover objects in their updated states after disappearance and reappearance [10]. More closely related to our setting, LongSpace-Bench includes scene consistency, state change, and route recall in long room-tour videos [31]. OVO-S-Bench evaluates scene revisit detection and counting under causal, prefix-only protocol, with visits in its counting task defined by location entering the field of view [33]. ReSpaceBench defines visits by physical room entry and deliberately includes distinct same-type rooms as competing identities along controlled revisit trajectories.

sections.title: 2.3 Persistent association and structured spatial memory.
sections.content: Persistent association underlies place recognition and loop closure in SLAM [8]. REMIND uses appearance, spatial context, and joint assignment for indoor object re-identification [15], while R4DSG indexes egocentric memory by time, place, persistent objects, and anchor-relative changes [38]. PBD-AG separates robot-verified structural baseline from revisable dynamic events [3], and GESTO uses event context within persistent 4D scene graph to refine object associations [4]. Complementing these methods, ReSpaceBench evaluates whether MLLMs can associate observations with persistent room identities and use visit histories and state information to answer questions across revisits.

sections.title: 3 ReSpaceBench
sections.content: ReSpaceBench evaluates persistent spatial memory through egocentric walkthrough that return to previously visited places. Its tasks span three task families  (Fig. 2)  : association, recognizing revisited room and matching it to an earlier observation; persistent state, maintaining room inventories, objectplace bindings, and object states across visits; and reasoning, inferring temporal order and spatial connectivity from this history. The benchmark evaluates these capabilities using rendered walkthroughs of synthetic and FARO-scanned homes, together with PICO headset recordings of real homes. Task overview. For association, T1 (query-to-memory association) matches query room to visited room or labels it as never entered; T2 (same-instance identification) identifies which previously visited same semantic type room is being revisited; and T3 (revisit counting) counts prior entries into specified room. For persistent state, T4 (room inventory) counts distinct visited rooms, overall or by semantic type, or determines rooms 4 Figure 2 Benchmark taxonomy: ReSpaceBench comprises 9 tasks across association (T1T3), persistent state (T4T7), and reasoning (T8T9). Representative questions and answers illustrate these tasks through room revisits, same-type room distractors, and cross-session state changes. position in the order of first visits; T5 (objectplace binding) reports first-visit of the first room containing an object of queried type; T6 (unique-object counting) counts distinct objects of queried type across revisits; and T7 (cross-session state) tracks object locations and changes across sessions in the same home. For reasoning, T8 (spatial topology) identifies room pairs directly connected by doorway, and T9 (temporal successor ) identifies the room type entered immediately after specified visit.

sections.title: 3.1 Benchmark Construction Pipeline
sections.content: Fig. 3(b) shows the 3 stages of benchmark construction. Scene metadata and camera trajectories connects each question to the rooms and objects observed in its video, providing shared and consistent basis for both question generation and answer verification. Scene collection, filtering, and metadata. To ensure that the benchmark poses meaningful spatial-memory challenges, we select large homes with diverse room layouts and multiple rooms of the same semantic type. We source synthetic household environments from 3D-FRONT [19], which provides professionally designed furnished apartments, and ProcTHOR [13], which contains procedurally generated homes. To complement these synthetic scenes, we scan real-world residential homes using FARO laser scanner and record egocentric activities with PICO headset. For synthetic scenes, we extract room geometry and semantic types, persistent room and object identities, object categories and locations, and doorway connectivity from the source metadata. For real homes, we manually annotate the corresponding information in the registered 3D scenes and align the annotations with the recorded egocentric trajectories. Route planning and egocentric video generation. We plan walkthrough routes using room layout to balance room coverage and controlled revisits. Task-specific configurations include visits to visually similar rooms of the same semantic type, episodes spanning single and multiple homes, and repeated sessions in the same home 5 Figure 3 Benchmark statistics and construction pipeline. (a) Question distribution across the 3 task families and 9 tasks. (b) The 3-stage construction pipeline for synthetic and real homes, with automated checks and human quality control. The camera path is illustrative. with controlled object changes. For both synthetic and scanned homes, we construct navigation meshes using Habitat Simulator [48]. Then, we adapt the navmesh-based navigation setup of Pred-EQA [67] to generate traversable paths that follow the planned room-entry sequences. We convert each path into continuous camera trajectory and render egocentric videos using BlenderProc [14], then concatenating videos across multiple homes when needed. Rendered walkthroughs use nominal walking speeds of 0.60.8 m/s. At each room entry, the camera pauses for 270 look-around lasting 69 seconds, providing sustained observations of the room. Hallways and stairwells are treated as transit spaces and are not counted as room visits. Each video is paired with camera poses, timestamps, room-entry events, and object-state records to support question generation, answer verification. Question generation from templates. We instantiate task-specific question templates using scene metadata, ordered room-entry sequences, and object-state records. The templates cover room association, room and object inventories, object to place binding, state changes, temporal order, and room connectivity. Rooms are referred to by semantic type when the type is unique within scene. Otherwise, we disambiguate them by order of first visit or unique visual cues (e.g., the second bedroom visited or the bedroom with wooden floor ). Ground-truth answers are deterministically derived from the corresponding scene annotations and realized trajectory. For multiple-choice questions, distractors are included to reflect plausible spatial-memory errors, such as confusing distinct rooms of the same type or inferring direct doorway connectivity from consecutive visits. Automatic and Human Quality Control. We verify each walkthrough by comparing the realized room-entry sequence with the planned route, rejecting trajectories with missing or unintended room entries. Ground-truth answers are then recomputed from the verified entry sequence and object-state records, and questions involving ambiguous visits or insufficient visual evidence are discarded. We further combine task-specific automated checks with manual inspection to assess rendering quality, room and object visibility, and consistency between the video and its metadata. During construction, shortcut diagnostics is implemented to examine answerfrequency biases, question and option wording, and room-type priors. These checks guide revisions to question 6 templates and answer balancing, while blind and frequency baselines provide additional diagnostics on the evaluation set. Training data. To support model development, we additionally provide RS-30K, training dataset of 30k questions generated from ProcTHOR training scenes. RS-30K uses separate set of question templates and shares no scenes, routes, or videos with ReSpaceBench. It provides targeted supervision without reusing evaluation environments or walkthroughs. We assess its utility through supervised fine-tuning of Qwen3-VL-8B, with results reported in Sec. 4.

sections.title: 3.2 Benchmark Statistics
sections.content: ReSpaceBench contains 3,244 evaluation questions, including 3,026 questions derived from synthetic environments and 218 questions from real homes. The real-home questions use 35 walkthrough videos rendered from FARO-scanned homes, which imitate egocentric videos by following the camera height, field of view, and motion of PICO recordings, and 13 videos from PICO headset recordings. Because FARO scan captures static scene, the PICO recordings are used for T7 (cross-session state), where objects change between sessions. Fig. 3(a) shows the distribution across 3 task families and 9 tasks. We additionally use ReSpaceBench-mini , 450-question subset containing 50 samples per task, for human evaluation, agentic experiments, and frame-sampling analyses (Sec. 4). RS-30K is separate training dataset and is therefore excluded from these evaluation statistics.

sections.title: 3.3 Evaluation Protocol
sections.content: Each model receives the walkthrough video and textual question, together with textual answer options for multiple-choice items. T1 additionally provides short query clip showing room from new viewpoint. The model must match this room to previously entered room or select the not entered option. Scene metadata, camera poses, and ground-truth event annotations are only for further analysis and not provided to models under the default evaluation protocol. Responses use one of two formats: an option letter for multiple-choice questions or value for numeric questions. Multiple-choice responses are scored by whether the selected option is correct, while numeric responses are scored by exact match to the ground-truth value. Overall accuracy is computed as the unweighted mean of the nine task accuracies. We report accuracy for each task and the average of each task family, alongside the Blind, Chance, and Frequency baselines described in Section 4.

sections.title: 4 Evaluations on ReSpaceBench
sections.content: We evaluate 32 models covering proprietary MLLMs, open-source general-purpose MLLMs, unified models, and specialized spatial and video-understanding models, as well as 3 agentic video-understanding frameworks. Except for targeted fine-tuning, models use their standard inference interfaces without benchmark-specific training. For direct inference, we sample videos at 1 fps by default, retaining approximately 69 views per room-entry look-around, and further downsample when required by model-specific context limits. Details are provided in the appendix. Blind, chance, and frequency baselines. Blind evaluates Seed 2.0 Pro with task instructions, questions, and answer options without any visual input. Chance averages 1/K over multiple-choice questions with options. Frequency predicts the most frequent ground-truth option letter or numeric value within each question subtype, with scores weighted by subtype question counts. It is computed from the evaluation answer distribution to quantify answer imbalance. All model responses follow the task-specific scoring rules (Section 3.3).

Human Evaluation. We evaluate three independent human annotators on ReSpaceBench-mini , with unrestricted video viewing and replay. Their mean accuracy reaches 90.1%, compared with 52.2% for GPT-5.6 Sol, difference of 37.9%. Human performance remains high across all nine tasks, supporting the benchmarks solvability. Agentic Video Understanding. We re-implement AVP [56], DVD [71], and VideoAgent [52] on ReSpaceBenchmini . To control for differences in backbone capabilities, we replace higher-capability models (e.g., Gemini 2.5 Pro, GPT-4 and o3) with GPT-5.6 Sol and lightweight models (e.g., Mini variants) with GPT-5.6 Luna, while retaining all other framework-specific configurations. Agents can access the full video and revisit segments through their respective tools. Under these configurations, none of the three frameworks outperform over direct inference. AVP and DVD each achieve 44.0%, while VideoAgent achieves 30.0%, compared with 52.2% for GPT-5.6 Sol (Tab. 3). Targeted Fine-Tuning. Fine-tuning Qwen3-VL-8B on our separate 30k-question training set raises overall accuracy from 35.5% to 60.4%, gain of 24.9 percentage points (Tab. 2). Accuracy improves on all nine tasks, with the largest gains in association and smaller, less consistent gains in persistent state and reasoning. The higher ProcTHOR accuracy may partly reflect similar design and furnishing styles within the dataset, despite no scene, route, or video overlap between training and evaluation. Average accuracy also improves on 3D-FRONT and real-world scenes, which are absent from fine-tuning, by 21.9 and 14.8 percentage points, respectively (Tab. 6). 4.2 Further Analysis
Can models distinguish rooms across revisits? We analyze T1 errors across the six proprietary models,
including the strongest zero-shot models. Errors comprise wrong room (choosing another visited room), false
merge (labeling an unentered room as visited), and false split (labeling an entered room as unentered). Wrong-
room selections dominate, accounting for 66.5–88.3% of errors (Figure 4(a)). False-split rates on visited-room
queries and false-merge rates on unvisited-room queries are below their respective uniform-random baselines
of 25.0% and 75.0% (Figure 4(b)). However, models still select an incorrect visited room in 44.8–58.0% of
visited-room queries. These results suggest that models can distinguish visited from unvisited rooms to some
extent, but often fail to identify which previously visited room the query depicts.
sections.content: Why do agentic frameworks fail? We manually inspect failed trajectories from AVP, DVD, and VideoAgent on ReSpaceBench-mini , reviewing their reasoning traces, tool calls, observed frames, and final answers (Fig. 4(c)). We identify four recurring major failure types: missing evidence, inaccurate observations, incorrect room-identity associations, and reasoning or verification errors. Trajectories with multiple problems are classified by the first observable error. AVP and DVD most often make errors in room identity association across revisit, whereas VideoAgent more frequently misses relevant evidence from video sequence. These findings suggest that evidence verification should check not only whether the necessary evidence has been retrieved, but also whether it has been interpreted correctly and linked to the correct room and visit. Does preserving event coverage improve performance? We compare uniform, most relevant event weighted, and event coverage aware sampling on ReSpaceBench-mini using GPT-5.6 Sol, with identical prompts and fixed budget of 128 frames. Both event-based strategies use walkthrough route annotations: event-weighted sampling assigns 4 the sampling weight to relevant room-entry events and coverage-aware sampling retains at least one frame from each room-entry, look-around, and hallway transitions interval. Coverage-aware sampling achieves 55.3%, compared with 47.6% for uniform and 47.8% for event-weighted sampling; the separate 1 fps baseline scores 52.2%  (Table 4)  . Omitting an intervening bedroom visit, for example, can make two bathroom visits appear continuous. These annotation-guided results suggest that preserving intervening visits and transitions helps distinguish revisits from continuous stays, highlighting the importance of event coverage alongside query-relevant observations.

sections.title: 5 Conclusion
sections.content: We introduced ReSpaceBench for evaluating persistent spatial memory across controlled revisits, together with RS-30K for targeted model training. Across synthetic and real homes, the benchmark evaluates room association, persistent state tracking, and downstream reasoning under viewpoint variation, identity ambiguity, and state changes. Our evaluations reveal substantial humanmodel gap and no overall advantage from the evaluated agentic frameworks. The analyses expose gap between recognizing room as familiar and linking it to the correct spatial memory, while annotation-guided sampling demonstrates the value of retaining intervening visits and transitions. Fine-tuning on RS-30K improves Qwen3-VL-8B from 35.5% to 60.4%, with gains extending to scene sources absent from training, but state tracking and reasoning benefit less consistently than association. These findings motivate spatial memory mechanisms that preserve room identity across viewpoints, distinguish visually similar rooms, and update memories as room and object states change, while retaining visit histories for downstream reasoning. We hope that ReSpaceBench, RS-30K together with the analysis can provide useful foundation for systematic evaluation, failure diagnosis, and targeted model development, and ultimately support further research toward more robust and generalizable persistent spatial memory and reasoning across revisits.

sections.title: A Implementation Details
sections.content: A.1 Model Evaluation Settings We resize video frames to 640 480 pixels and initially sample at 1 fps for default setting for all evaluated models. Due to model-specific context-length limits, we further uniformly downsample the sampled sequence when necessary, retaining the maximum number of frames that each model can accommodate alongside the question, answer options, reference inputs, and reserved response tokens. Sequences that fit are used in full. All retained frames preserve their chronological order. For multi-home visit questions, the context budget covers all sequences jointly. sections.title: B Data Construction and Question Definitions
sections.content: Room entries and persistent identity. Room entries are recovered from the rendered camera trajectory and its room labels. visit requires entering room; viewing it through doorway does not count. Re-entry into the same physical room creates new visit while preserving its identity. The initial countable room is included as the first visit, and hallways, corridors, stairs, and other transit spaces are excluded. Room inventories and first-encounter ordinals count each physical room once, whereas revisit counts retain separate entry events. Ground-truth verification. Answers are recomputed from the verified room-entry sequence and object-state records. For entry-dependent questions, we check the annotated entry order against the recorded look-arounds. Questions with inconsistent annotations or ambiguous room references are excluded. Object counts use persistent instance identities to avoid counting the same object again on revisit. Task-specific evidence validation. To ensure disambiguity in synthetic scene annotations, room labels are checked against the furnishings and fixtures present after scene preparation. T1 (query-to-memory association) verifies whether the query room was entered, and T9 (temporal successor) uses the realized order of countable-room entries. Object related questions additionally applies geometric visibility and image-quality checks to the queried objects over multiple frames, with further framing and occlusion checks for reference images. Only visible objects in the video are counted towards the ground-truth. 19 B.1 Task Subtypes and Templates Table 7 summarizes the task definitions and gives representative question wording from the evaluation set. The exact instant of entering or leaving room may fall between two sampled frames, but temporally adjacent observations remain available. Moreover, each counted visit includes an in-room look-around lasting 69 seconds, which provides approximately 69 sampled views under the full 1 fps setting. B.3 Shortcut Controls During Construction The construction pipeline includes several checks to reduce non-visual shortcuts [5]. At the question level, the question text does not state information that must be recalled from the video. We balance the option letters (A/B/C/D) as well as the answer content, such as the room type (bathroom/bedroom/living room) or the ordinal option (first/second/not entered). Questions with the same wording and the same options are paired with different visual inputs that lead to different answers, so that answering depends on the video. Distractors are rooms of the same type that appear in the same video, so they cannot be excluded by common sense. We further check for priors and textual shortcuts by testing strategies that guess fixed answer from the room type or object category, or that answer from option length, lexicographic order, or ordinal words. After rendering, visibility, and quality filtering, we repeat these checks on the resulting answer distributions, so that filtering does not reintroduce biases.

Visual-input condition Nine-task average (%) Correct visual input No visual input (blind) Randomly mismatched visual input 60.4 29.6 20. To further test whether the fine-tuned model relies on textual shortcuts or on visual evidence, we evaluate the same checkpoint on all 3,244 questions under three conditions with matched evaluation settings: the correct visual input, no visual input (blind ), and randomly mismatched visual input. In the mismatched condition, the visual input of each question is replaced with that of randomly sampled question from different scene whose ground-truth answer differs. As shown in Tab. 9, removing the visual input reduces accuracy by 30.8 points, and mismatched inputs reduce it by further 8.8 points. The fine-tuned model therefore relies substantially on visual evidence rather than on textual shortcuts. C.2 Does Identity Association Limit Cross-Session State Tracking? Table 10 Identity-oracle analysis on T7 (cross-session state) with GPT-5.6 Sol on all 559 T7 questions. Gains are in percentage points over the original input. Visual input Accuracy (%) Gain Original input + Room type and persistent room ID + Object masks and consistent instance IDs 47.0 51.9 54.0 +4.9 +7.0 We run an identity-oracle analysis on cross-session state (T7). The task requires identifying the room and the object before comparing their states. To test whether identity association limits performance, we evaluate GPT-5.6 Sol on all 559 T7 questions while providing ground-truth identity (Tab. 10). The room oracle annotates each frame with its room type and unique room ID. The room + object oracle additionally overlays object masks with unique instance IDs onto the frames. These annotations provide identity correspondence without revealing object states, state changes, or ground-truth answers. Providing room IDs improves accuracy by 4.9 points, and adding object-level annotations yields total gain of 7.0 points. These results suggest that identity correspondence is one source of difficulty in cross-session state-change reasoning, while substantial errors remain even when ground-truth identity cues are provided. Improving ReSpaceBench alone does not fully establish generalization. Fine-tuning on RS-30K alone substantially improves ReSpaceBench but reduces performance on some external benchmarks, limitation of training exclusively on task-specific data. We therefore study mixed-data fine-tuning, following the common 22 practice of combining specialized and general instruction data in spatial MLLM training, as in MM-Spatial [12] and SpatialRGPT [11]. With the same Qwen3-VL-8B [44] backbone, we fine-tune on partial VLM-3R [16] and LLaVA-Video [73] data, with and without RS-30K. Table 11 reports the results. Adding RS-30K improves VSI-Bench [60] and its debiased subset [5] by 2.4 and 1.1 points, respectively, and raises ReSpaceBench accuracy to 63.6%, gain of 28.1 points over the original model. Video-MME [18] reaches 67.6%, above both the mixture without RS-30K and the original model. Combined with broader training data, RS-30K thus provides spatial-memory supervision without sacrificing performance on the evaluated external benchmarks.
